checked_sources: Basistha--Ionascu, Permutations of N and primorial numbers / arXiv:2302.02838 and 2025 journal version
correctness.rationale: For consecutive records r<r', the recurrence gives r'-r=ell(r-1)-1. A skipped target x congruent to 25 mod 30 cannot lie in a gap with ell=3 by parity, nor with ell=5 because ell=5 forces r≡1 mod 6 while x=r+2 and x≡25 mod 30 would force r≡5 mod 6. If ell>=7 then r≡1 mod 30; swallowing the next 25 mod 30 residue requires x-r>=24 and hence ell>=29, which forces every prime through 23 to divide r-1. Thus 23# divides r-1 and no target below 23#+25 can be skipped. For P=23#, P+1 is a record: if it were skipped after a preceding record r, a common prime divisor of P+1 and r-1 would be at least 29, leaving room to insert r-1+q for a prime q<=23 not dividing r-1, contradicting consecutiveness. Since ell(P)=29, the next record after P+1 is P+29, so P+25 is skipped. Independent arithmetic reconfirmed P=223092870, P/30=7436429 and the next missing prime 29.

value.rationale: The primary source itself highlights the period-30 multiples-of-5 record pattern while asking for composite-record structure. The result identifies the exact first boundary of that observed phenomenon—after more than seven million consecutive terms—and explains it structurally by the first record gap whose missing-prime parameter reaches 29. This is a motivated exact cutoff rather than an arbitrary finite check.
